title: Mixed Conditionals
body_content:
Practice Mixed Conditionals.

Say it: 'd have and 'd in mixed conditionals

In mixed conditionals the contracted forms blur: I'd have /aɪd əv/ and I'd /aɪd/ sound almost the same. Have is reduced to /əv/. Stress the two key verbs: If I'd STUDied law, I'd be a LAWyer now.

Say it: "If I'd taken that job, I'd be living abroad now."

audio_urls.title: Say it: 'd have and 'd in mixed conditionals

title: Inversion
body_content:
Practice Inversion.

Say it: stress in negative inversion

After a fronted negative adverbial the auxiliary comes before the subject, and the fronted phrase takes the stress: NEVer have I SEEN such a mess. Pause briefly after the fronted phrase, then keep the rest smooth: Not ONly did she WIN | but she broke the RECord.

Say it: "Under no circumstances should you open this door."

audio_urls.title: Say it: stress in negative inversion

title: Modal Perfect
body_content:
Practice Modal Perfect.

Say it: modal perfect: have is weak

In modal perfects have is reduced to /əv/ and often sounds like of: should have /ʃʊd əv/, might have /maɪt əv/. Write have, never of. Stress the modal for judgement and the participle for content: You SHOULD have TOLD me.

Where accents differ

UKneedn't have gone
USdidn't need to go (more common)
Say it: "She must have left. He can't have known. You should have told me."

audio_urls.title: Say it: modal perfect: have is weak

title: Causative
body_content:
Practice Causative.

Say it: have / get something done

Stress the thing done and the participle: I had my HAIR CUT. I'm getting the CAR serviced. Have is usually weak: I'll have it fixed /aɪl həv ɪt fɪkst/.

Where accents differ

UKI'm having the boiler serviced.
I had my flat repainted.
USI'm getting the furnace serviced.
I got my apartment painted.
Say it: "She had her passport renewed. We're getting the roof repaired."

audio_urls.title: Say it: have / get something done

title: Concession
body_content:
Practice Concession.

Listen for: concession in speech

Though at the end of a sentence is a common spoken concession, often with a fall-rise: It was expensive. Worth it, though. However is usually followed by a pause. After although, listen for the stressed contrast: Although it was RAINing, we went OUT.

Where accents differ

UKAll the same, even so
Mind you (informal): Mind you, it was cheap.
USStill, even so
Then again: Then again, it was cheap.
Listen for: "Nice hotel. Noisy, though. Even so, we'd go back."

title: Habit in the Present and the Past

revision.summary: Practice Habit in the Present and the Past.

body_content:
Practice Habit in the Present and the Past.

Listen for: used to and would for habits

Used to is /ˈjuːst tə/ (the d disappears): We used to LIVE there. Would for past habits is contracted: We'd go every SUMmer. Listen for time words such as every, always and when I was young.

Where accents differ

UKI used not to (formal)
I usedn't to (rare)
USI didn't use to
I never used to
Listen for: "We used to go every summer. We'd swim before breakfast."

audio_urls.title: Listen for: used to and would for habits

revision.summary: Practice Present Perfect Simple and Continuous.

title: Past Simple, Past Continuous, Past Perfect

revision.summary: Practice Past Simple, Past Continuous, Past Perfect.

body_content:
Practice Past Simple, Past Continuous, Past Perfect.

Say it: -ed endings and 'd had

The past simple -ed has three sounds: /t/ after voiceless sounds (worked), /d/ after voiced sounds (played /pleɪd/), /ɪd/ after /t/ or /d/ (wanted). In the past perfect, had is weak or contracted: She'd already left /ʃiːd ɔːlˈredi left/.

Where accents differ

UKworked /wɜːkt/
wanted /ˈwɒntɪd/
USworked /wɜːrkt/
wanted /ˈwɑːntɪd/
Say it: "I worked all day. I'd already finished when she arrived."

title: Question tags
body_content:
Practice Question tags.

Say it: question tags: agree or ask

A falling tag seeks agreement: Nice day, isn't it ↘. A rising tag is a real question: You're coming, aren't you ↗? Keep the tag short and light: /ˈɪznt ɪt/.

Where accents differ

UKI'm late, aren't I?
Let's go, shall we?
USI'm late, aren't I?
Let's go, okay?
Say it: "It's cold, isn't it? You haven't seen it, have you?"

audio_urls.title: Say it: question tags: agree or ask

title: Future forms
body_content:
Practice Future forms.

Say it: 'll, going to and present continuous

Going to often sounds like gonna /ˈɡʌnə/ in speech. I'll /aɪl/ is quick and light: I'll call you. The present continuous for plans stresses the time: I'm meeting her on FRIday. Write going to in formal writing.

Say it: "I'll call you later. I'm going to study. We're meeting on Friday."

audio_urls.title: Say it: 'll, going to and present continuous

title: Future Perfect
body_content:
Practice Future Perfect.

Say it: 'll have in the future perfect

Will have shrinks to 'll have /əl əv/: By June I'll have finished /baɪ dʒuːn aɪl əv ˈfɪnɪʃt/. Stress the time expression and the participle: By FRIday, they'll have FINished.

Say it: "By this time next year, she'll have graduated."

audio_urls.title: Say it: 'll have in the future perfect

revision.summary: Practice Zero, first, second, third conditionals.

title: Wish and if only
body_content:
Practice Wish and if only.

Say it: I wish I were / was

Both I wish I were and I wish I was are used; were is more formal. Reduce I wish I and stress the wished-for idea. If only is stressed strongly: If ONly I had more TIME.

Say it: "I wish I were taller. If only I had listened."

audio_urls.title: Say it: I wish I were / was

title: Compounds of some, any, no, every

revision.summary: Practice Compounds of some, any, no, every.

title: Relative clauses
body_content:
Practice Relative clauses.

Listen for: pauses in relative clauses

Non-defining clauses are set off by pauses (commas in writing): My brother, | who lives in Leeds, | is a nurse. Defining clauses have no pauses: The man who lives next door is a nurse. The pauses change the meaning: the first suggests I have only one brother.

Listen for: "My sister, who lives in Rome, is a doctor. The sister who lives in Rome is a doctor."

audio_urls.title: Listen for: pauses in relative clauses

title: Conjunctions: although, despite, in spite of, otherwise, unless

revision.summary: Practice Conjunctions: although, despite, in spite of, otherwise, unless.

body_content:
Practice Conjunctions: although, despite, in spite of, otherwise, unless.

Listen for: although, despite, unless

Although is stressed on the second syllable: alTHOUGH it was late. Despite and in spite of are followed by a noun or -ing: despite the RAIN. Unless /ənˈles/ is weak at the start.

Where accents differ

UKalthough /ɔːlˈðəʊ/
whilst (formal)
USalthough /ɔːlˈðoʊ/
while
Listen for: "Although it was late, we stayed. Unless it rains, we'll go."

revision.summary: Practice Adverbs of manner and modifiers.

title: Affixes
body_content:
Practice Affixes.

Say it: stress with suffixes

Some suffixes move stress: PHOtograph → phoTOGrapher → photoGRAPHic. -tion and -ic put stress on the syllable before: eduCAtion, ecoNOMic. Prefixes like un-, re-, dis- usually keep the stress: HAPpy → unHAPpy.

Where accents differ

UKsecretary /ˈsekrətri/
missile /ˈmɪsaɪl/
USsecretary /ˈsekrəteri/
missile /ˈmɪsl/
Say it: "photograph, photographer, photographic; economy, economic."

title: Crime and punishment — B2 legal process

revision.summary: Practice Crime and punishment — B2 legal process.

title: Relationships
body_content:
Practice Relationships.

Listen for: closeness in tone

The same words can sound close or distant. We're just friends. with a fall sounds final; with a fall-rise it leaves doubt. Listen for stress on just and really: We're JUST friends.

Where accents differ

UKget on with someone
fancy someone
USget along with someone
have a crush on someone
Listen for: "We get on really well. We're just friends."

title: Festivals and celebrations
body_content:
Practice Festivals and celebrations.

Listen for: festival vocabulary and stress

Stress in festival words: CELebrate, celeBRAtion, FEStival, TRAdition, fireworks /ˈfaɪəwɜːks/. Listen for stress on the event name and the day in invitations: See you at the PARty on SAturday.

Where accents differ

UKBonfire Night, Boxing Day
USFourth of July, Thanksgiving
Listen for: "The festival starts on Friday. Fireworks begin at nine."

audio_urls.title: Listen for: festival vocabulary and stress

title: Idiomatic expressions
body_content:
Practice Idiomatic expressions.

Listen for: idioms in connected speech

Idioms are often said as one chunk, with the stress on the last content word: it's a piece of CAKE, let's call it a DAY. Expect reductions: a piece of /ə ˈpiːs əv/. Listen for the chunk, not the individual words.

Where accents differ

UKa storm in a teacup
bob's your uncle
USa tempest in a teapot
hit a home run
Listen for: "It's a piece of cake. Let's call it a day."

audio_urls.title: Listen for: idioms in connected speech

title: Geography and climate
body_content:
Practice Geography and climate.

Say it: place names and climate words

English place names often break spelling rules: Thames /temz/, Worcester /ˈwʊstə/, Arctic /ˈɑːktɪk/ (say the first c). Learn stress for climate words: CLImate, TROpical, TEMperature.

Where accents differ

UKtropical /ˈtrɒpɪkl/
temperature /ˈtemprətʃə/
UStropical /ˈtrɑːpɪkl/
temperature /ˈtemprətʃər/
Say it: "The Thames is cold. The Arctic climate is harsh."

audio_urls.title: Say it: place names and climate words

title: Expressing regret
body_content:
Practice Expressing regret.

Say it: regret in your voice

Regret uses a falling tone and stress on the key word: I WISH I'd said something. If only I'd LISTened. Have is weak: I should have called /aɪ ʃʊd əv kɔːld/. A slower pace and lower pitch sound sincere.

Say it: "I should have called. I wish I'd listened."

audio_urls.title: Say it: regret in your voice

title: Stating contrast — conversational
body_content:
Practice Stating contrast — conversational.

Listen for: contrast in conversation

Spoken contrast: Yeah, but... starts a disagreement, Still,... accepts a point then reverses it. Listen for a fall-rise on the first idea and a fall on the contrast: It's ↘↗cheap, but it's ↘slow.

Where accents differ

UKMind you, it's cheap.
USThen again, it's cheap.
Listen for: "It's cheap, but it's slow. Still, it works."

title: Clarifying
body_content:
Practice Clarifying.

Say it: checking and clarifying

To check you understood, use a rising tone: So you mean the FIRST one? To ask for repetition politely: Sorry, could you say that again? To correct, stress the changed word: Not Tuesday, THURSday.

Where accents differ

UKSorry? / Pardon?
USExcuse me? / Come again? (informal)
Say it: "Sorry, do you mean the first one? Not Tuesday, Thursday."

title: Connected Speech

revision.summary: Learn how sounds change, disappear or join in fast speech (assimilation, elision, weak forms) so you can speak fluently and understand native speakers.

body_content:
Connected Speech

In careful speech every word is separate. In real speech, sounds change to make speaking easier. Learning these patterns helps you understand fast speakers and sound more natural.

1. Elision: sounds disappear

A /t/ or /d/ between two consonants often disappears: next day = "nex day", old man = "ol man", last night = "las night". Also inside words: friendship = "frenship".

2. Assimilation: sounds change

A sound becomes more like the next one: handbag = "hambag", ten pounds = "tem pounds", good boy = "goob boy", this shop = "thish shop".

3. Weak forms and contractions

Grammar words shrink: and = /ən/, of = /əv/, have = /əv/ in should have = "should've". Informal spelling shows this: gonna, wanna, gotta. Use them to understand, and be careful in formal writing.

4. Where accents differ

Both accents connect speech, but the patterns are not the same:

UKa lot of = "a lot ov" (t is clear)
Have you got...? is common
Shall we?
USa lot of = "a lodda" (t sounds like d)
Do you have...? is common
Should we?
Practice tip: record a short sentence at natural speed and compare it with the written words. Note which sounds disappear.

title: Contrastive Stress

revision.summary: Learn to move the main stress to a word to correct, contrast or emphasise information, and to hear the speaker's meaning from where the stress falls.
examples: I didn't say HE stole it.

body_content:
Contrastive Stress

Normally the main stress falls on the last content word: I bought a new CAR. With contrastive stress you move it to show a contrast, a correction or a surprise.

1. Correcting information

A: Is the meeting on Monday? B: No, it's on TUESday. The stressed word is the new information.

2. Showing a contrast

I like TEA, but she likes COFFEE. Both stressed words are the pair being compared.

3. One sentence, different meanings

Say "I didn't say he stole it" seven times, stressing a different word each time. Each version means something different: I didn't say it (someone else did); I didn't say it (I wrote it); he stole (he borrowed).

4. Numbers and letters

Stress the part that is different: fifTEEN or FIFty; B as in Bravo, not P. This is very useful on the phone.

5. Where accents differ

Contrastive stress works the same in both accents. Some words that you contrast may differ:

UKfortnight (two weeks) not week
flat, not house
autumn, not summer
UStwo weeks, not one week
apartment, not house
fall, not summer
Practice tip: correct a false statement out loud. "It's in Paris." "No, it's in ROME."

title: UK and US: /r/ and /t/

revision.summary: Compare how British and American English say /r/ after vowels and /t/ between vowels (flapping, glottal stops), so you can recognise both and choose one to use.

body_content:
UK and US: /r/ and /t/

The two biggest differences between standard British and American pronunciation are the letter r and the letter t. Knowing the rules makes both accents easy to understand.

1. The letter r

American English is rhotic: r is always pronounced. Standard British English is non-rhotic: r is pronounced only before a vowel.

UKcar = /kɑː/
park = /pɑːk/
teacher = /ˈtiːtʃə/
car alarm = /kɑːr əˈlɑːm/ (linking r)
UScar = /kɑːr/
park = /pɑːrk/
teacher = /ˈtiːtʃər/
car alarm = /kɑːr əˈlɑːrm/

2. The letter t between vowels

In American English /t/ between two vowels (when the second is unstressed) becomes a quick flap like a soft /d/: water, better, city. So latter and ladder sound almost the same.

UKwater = /ˈwɔːtə/ (clear t)
better = /ˈbetə/
bottle = often /ˈbɒʔl/ (glottal stop in informal speech)
USwater = /ˈwɔːɾər/ (flap)
better = /ˈbeɾər/
bottle = /ˈbɑːɾl/

3. Which to learn?

Choose one accent as your model and stay consistent. Practise recognising the other by listening to films, podcasts and news from both countries.

Practice tip: say "better butter" in both ways: with a clear t (UK) and a flap (US).

title: Listening: Podcasts

revision.summary: Practise listening to conversational podcasts, following opinions, informal language and jumps in topic, with UK and US vocabulary differences.
examples: To be honest, I wasn't convinced.
Anyway, going back to what I said...

body_content:
Listening: Podcasts

Podcasts are natural and informal. Speakers interrupt, change topic and use fillers. To follow them, listen for the topic, each speaker's opinion and the discourse markers that show the structure.

1. Script 1: two hosts

A: So, what did you think of the new city bike scheme?
B: To be honest, I wasn't convinced at first. I mean, the bikes are heavy. But actually, after a week I was hooked.
A: Really? Anyway, the price is what surprised me. A pound for thirty minutes!
B: Right, which is cheaper than the bus.

Opinions: B changes from not convinced to hooked. A is surprised by the price.

2. Discourse markers

  • To be honest, I mean, actually = the speaker gives an opinion or correction.
  • Anyway = change topic or return to the topic.
  • Right, exactly, I know = agreement.
  • By the way = a side comment.

3. Script 2: a story

So last week I was driving to work, and, you won't believe this, a lorry stopped in front of me and the driver got out to buy a sandwich! I mean, in the middle of the road!

Notice So (start of a story) and you won't believe this (something surprising). The listener does not need to catch every word.

4. Where UK and US differ

UKlorry, flat, mate
I reckon
quite good = fairly good
UStruck, apartment, buddy
I guess
pretty good = fairly good
Practice tip: play a podcast for two minutes, then write the topic, one opinion and the discourse markers you noticed.

title: Listening: Lectures and Note-taking

revision.summary: Practise listening to short lectures and taking notes: catching the main idea, signposts, key terms and examples, and writing them down with abbreviations.
examples: e.g. = for example; i.e. = that is

body_content:
Listening: Lectures and Note-taking

Lecturers give a lot of information in a short time. You cannot write every word. You need to listen for structure and write only key words.

1. Listen for signposts

  • Today I'll talk about... = topic.
  • There are three main causes = number of points.
  • First, second, finally = order.
  • This means that, in other words = an explanation.
  • For example = an example.
  • To sum up = the conclusion.

2. Script: a short lecture

Today I'll talk about urban heat islands. Cities are often hotter than the countryside, and there are two main causes. First, dark surfaces like roads absorb heat. Second, there are fewer trees, which means less shade and less cooling. For example, some cities are up to five degrees warmer at night. To sum up, planting trees and using lighter materials can help.

3. Model notes

Topic: urban heat islands (cities hotter)
Causes: 1) dark surfaces absorb heat 2) fewer trees = less shade
Ex: up to 5° warmer at night
Solution: trees + light materials

4. Abbreviations and symbols

e.g. = for example; i.e. = that is; = = means; → = leads to; w/ = with; & = and. Use numbers instead of words and keep only nouns, verbs and numbers.

5. Where UK and US differ

UKlecturer, module, revise for an exam
Uni / university
maths
USprofessor, course, review for a test
college / school (university)
math
Practice tip: after each lecture, rewrite your notes in a clear format and cover them to see what you remember.

title: Listening: Accents

revision.summary: Practise understanding different accents (British, American, Australian, Indian and others) by listening for stress and key words, with strategies for when speech is unfamiliar.
examples: Could you say that again, please?

body_content:
Listening: Accents

English is spoken by more people as a second language than as a first language. You will hear many accents at work, on trips and online. Every accent is different, but the grammar and stressed words are similar.

1. Strategies

  • Focus on stressed words.
  • Use context: topic, situation, gestures.
  • Expect the same word to sound different: a different vowel, a different r, a different t.
  • Ask politely: Sorry, I didn't catch that. Could you say it again, please?

2. Some typical patterns

  • Scottish and Irish English: r is often rolled or clear; vowels are often shorter.
  • Australian English: "day" sounds nearer to "die"; the rising tone is common on statements.
  • Indian English: syllables have similar length, and t and d are often made with the tongue touching the teeth.
  • General American: r is clear, t between vowels is a flap.

3. Script: a conversation between two accents

A (Australian): G'day! Are you free at three?
B (American): Three? Sorry, I didn't catch that. Did you say three or thirty?
A: Three. No worries, I'll say it again: at three o'clock.
B: Got it. See you then.

Note: B checks the number and A repeats it clearly. This is a good real-life strategy.

4. Where UK and US differ

UKSorry? or Pardon?
Cheers = thanks / goodbye
How do you do?
USExcuse me? or What was that?
Thanks
How are you doing?
Practice tip: each week watch a short video from a different English-speaking country and note two sounds that are different.
